title: Nobody in Shanghai Wants Your Cash. Here Are Your Four Real Options.
summary: Cash gets sighs, foreign cards get declined, and WeChat Pay runs the country. A frank comparison of how visitors can actually pay in China in 2026.
body_markdown:
There is a specific moment most first time visitors to China remember. You finish a bowl of noodles, pull out a crisp 100 yuan note, and the owner looks at it like you handed her a fax machine. She points at a laminated QR code taped to the counter. You do not have WeChat Pay. She does not have change. Everyone waits.


China is the most cashless large economy on earth, and it got there without card terminals. The entire country runs on two apps, WeChat Pay and Alipay, and on the QR codes they read. Taxis, street vendors, temples, vending machines, even buskers take payment by QR. That is wonderful if you live there. It is a genuine problem if you just landed with a foreign card and a wallet full of paper.


So let's compare the actual options honestly, because each one works differently in China than it does anywhere else in Asia.


## Option one: cash, the backup that keeps apologizing


Cash is still legal tender, and by law merchants are supposed to accept it. In practice, you will meet drivers with no change, market stalls that wave you toward the QR sign, and younger staff who genuinely have not handled a banknote in months. You can usually make cash work at larger supermarkets, hotels, and tourist sites, but it turns every small purchase into a negotiation.


Getting that cash is its own ordeal. You need an ATM that accepts foreign cards, which narrows you to major banks in major cities, and then you pay the usual stack: the local machine's fee, your home bank's foreign ATM fee, and whatever rate gets applied to the withdrawal. In countries like


[Thailand, where going ATM free is now realistic](https://moretapay.com/blog/thailand-avoid-atm-fees-bad-exchange-rates-promptpay-qr-2026-2026-10-10)


, cash is at least welcomed when you have it. In China you pay all those fees for money people would rather not take.


**Verdict:**


carry a small amount for emergencies and the rare cash only situation. Do not build your trip on it.


## Option two: your foreign Visa or Mastercard


Here is the part that surprises travelers who have been everywhere else in Asia. Foreign card acceptance in China is minimal outside international hotel chains, airport shops, and some upscale restaurants in Beijing and Shanghai. The country skipped the card era almost entirely. Domestic payments went from cash straight to QR, so the terminal you are hoping to tap simply does not exist at the noodle shop, the tea stall, or in the taxi.


Even where a terminal exists, it often only speaks UnionPay, the domestic card network. Your Visa or Mastercard might work at the Marriott front desk and nowhere else all day. And when it does work, you are still exposed to whatever foreign transaction fees your issuer charges and any dynamic currency conversion tricks at checkout.


**Verdict:**


useful for the hotel bill. Nearly useless for daily life.


## Option three: setting up WeChat Pay or Alipay yourself


This is the path locals will suggest, and it deserves a fair hearing. Both apps have opened up to international visitors in recent years, letting you link a foreign card instead of a Chinese bank account. When it works, you are paying exactly like a local, scanning the same codes at the same stalls.


The honest downsides: the setup involves identity verification steps that can stall, the experience sits inside apps designed for a domestic audience, and the costs are not always obvious up front. You are also routing your spending through a foreign card linked deep inside an unfamiliar app, which some travelers are comfortable with and others are not. For a long stay or an expat posting, investing an afternoon in setup can absolutely be worth it. For a one or two week trip, plenty of visitors give up halfway through verification in the airport arrivals hall.


**Verdict:**


the most local option, with real friction and less transparency than most travelers expect.


## Option four: a wallet that reads China's QR codes but behaves like your bank at home


This is the category Moreta Pay sits in, and the comparison is straightforward. You top up a wallet in your own currency before or during the trip, from a US bank via Plaid or ACH, a European SEPA account, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card. In China, you scan the same WeChat Pay QR code the person ahead of you scanned. The app shows you the amount, the merchant name, and the exact FX rate before you confirm anything. Tap confirm, the merchant is paid instantly in yuan, and you walk off with your noodles.


What you give up compared to a native WeChat Pay setup is full membership in the Chinese app ecosystem (mini programs, in-app services, chat). What you gain is a setup that takes minutes instead of an afternoon, pricing you can read before every payment instead of discovering on a statement, and no need for a Chinese phone number or local bank account. Because the same wallet reads


[local QR standards across Asia and Latin America](https://moretapay.com/blog/how-to-pay-with-qr-codes-as-a-foreigner-in-cambodia)


, it keeps working after your flight out of Pudong, which matters if China is one stop on a longer route.


**Verdict:**


the lowest friction way for a visitor to join China's QR economy, especially on shorter trips or multi country itineraries.


## Where each option actually wins


**The taxi at midnight:**


QR or nothing. Drivers often carry no change and no card machine. Cash loses, foreign cards lose, any working QR wallet wins.


**The street market in Chengdu:**


every stall has a printed code and nobody has small bills. Same result.


**The five star hotel:**


your foreign card finally gets its moment. Use it here if you like.


**Booking trains, hotels, and shopping online:**


platforms like Trip.com lean heavily on QR based checkout for local payment methods. Moreta Pay handles QR payments on travel and shopping platforms too, which closes the loop for the planning half of your trip, not just the street level half.


**The remote village day trip:**


this is where a few hundred yuan in cash earns its place in your pocket. Keep it there, mostly untouched, as insurance.


## A workable plan for your first week


Withdraw one modest round of cash at a major bank ATM at the airport, treat it as emergency money, and do not plan a second run. Put your foreign card to work only at hotels and big ticket bookings. For everything else, the dozens of small daily payments that actually make up a trip to China, get yourself onto QR before you need it. If you have the patience and a long stay ahead, set up WeChat Pay or Alipay directly. If you want to land ready,
